title: India's Commerce Minister Is in Switzerland Today to Push a Trade Deal That Could Reshape Pharma Access for Millions.
excerpt: Piyush Goyal meets the Swiss President and pharma industry leaders in Berne to accelerate the India-EFTA trade pact that has been operational since October 2025 but has yet to deliver on its investment promises.
body:
Piyush Goyal landed in Berne on Thursday with a trade deal that exists on paper and a bilateral relationship that needs results on the ground. India's Commerce and Industry Minister is spending two days in Switzerland meeting the country's Federal President Guy Parmelin, State Secretary for Economic Affairs Helene Budliger Artieda, and senior figures from the Swiss pharmaceutical industry.

The agenda is the India-EFTA Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement, or TEPA — signed in March 2024, operational since October 2025 — and the growing gap between its ambitions and its delivery.

## What TEPA Promised

The agreement between India and the four European Free Trade Association nations — Switzerland, Norway, Liechtenstein and Iceland — was hailed as a landmark when it was signed. EFTA countries committed to facilitating $100 billion in investment into India over 15 years. In return, India granted market access on 92.2 per cent of EFTA tariff lines, covering 99.6 per cent of India's exports to the bloc.

Bilateral merchandise trade between India and Switzerland stood at approximately $23.35 billion in the 2024-25 fiscal year. But the relationship is deeply lopsided: India exported about $1.47 billion worth of goods to Switzerland while importing $21.88 billion — much of it gold and pharmaceutical intermediates.

The investment commitment was supposed to begin rebalancing this equation. Eight months after TEPA became operational, the question in Berne is whether the pipeline is materialising.

## Why Pharma Is the Real Conversation

Goyal's meetings with Swiss pharmaceutical industry leaders are the most consequential part of the visit. Switzerland is home to Novartis, Roche, and several other global pharma giants whose pricing decisions ripple through India's healthcare system — the world's largest producer of generic drugs.

The tension has always been structural. Switzerland wants stronger intellectual property protections and longer patent exclusivity periods in India. India wants Swiss pharma companies to invest in manufacturing capacity on Indian soil rather than simply selling finished products at premium prices. TEPA was supposed to provide a framework for navigating this tension. The Berne meetings will reveal whether that framework is holding.

For the Indian diaspora, the pharma dimension is personal. NRI families routinely manage healthcare across two systems, often relying on Indian generics for conditions where branded drugs in the US, UK or Canada are prohibitively expensive. Any tightening of IP rules under TEPA could affect the availability and pricing of the generics they depend on.

## The Broader Trade Context

Goyal arrives in Switzerland at a moment when India is simultaneously negotiating trade agreements on multiple fronts. A bilateral trade deal with the United States is moving towards a first tranche that could close by mid-July, according to Goyal's own statements last week. Modi is expected to discuss trade terms with Trump at the G7 summit in Evian-les-Bains next week.

Washington has proposed an additional 12.5 per cent tariff on Indian imports, alleging the use of forced labour — a charge India has rejected. Against this backdrop, demonstrating that the EFTA deal is working becomes a useful piece of evidence that India can execute complex trade agreements and honour their terms.

This is Goyal's second engagement with Switzerland in 2026. In February, he met Parmelin in New Delhi to review the implementation roadmap. Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agarwal visited Berne in May for working-level discussions on translating TEPA's market access provisions into actual business partnerships.

## What to Watch

The visit is expected to produce commitments on three fronts: resolving operational issues that have emerged since TEPA became effective, identifying specific sectors for expanded bilateral investment, and deepening institutional cooperation between Indian and Swiss regulatory bodies.

Goyal will also meet Swiss companies and investors in Zurich to discuss trade and investment opportunities. He is accompanied by officials from the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade and the Ministry of Health — a signal that pharmaceutical regulation is on the table.

The real measure of success will not be in the joint statements. It will be in whether Swiss investment flows into India accelerate in the next two quarters, and whether the pharma pricing conversation produces outcomes that both sides can present as wins.
